title: NLRB v. Hearst Publications, Inc.
lead: Regular Los Angeles street vendors organized and sought bargaining, while publishers called them independent contractors. The Court examined their economic relationships and the Board’s role in applying a national labor statute.

actors.name: Four Los Angeles newspaper publishers
actors.role: Employers challenged in four companion cases, including two Hearst cases, Stockholders Publishing, and Times-Mirror.

actors.name: Regular full-time street vendors
actors.role: Generally adult livelihood-dependent sellers conventionally called newsboys; the workers whose status was at issue.

actors.name: Los Angeles Newsboys union
actors.role: Petitioned for elections and certification and demanded bargaining after winning.

actors.name: National Labor Relations Board
actors.role: NLRB; classified the designated workers as employees, selected units, and issued bargaining orders.

proceedings: Board held consolidated representation hearings, ordered elections, and certified the union after majority wins.
Publishers refused bargaining; Board unfair-labor-practice proceedings produced cease-and-desist and bargaining orders.
Ninth Circuit set orders aside over a dissent.
Supreme Court on April 24, 1944 reversed and remanded all four causes 8–1; Reed concurred in result and Roberts dissented.
limits: The case concerns designated regular street vendors under the 1944 statute, not every dealer, child seller, newsstand, or delivery carrier. It does not resolve later amended employment definitions or adopt later courts’ characterizations of its deference reasoning.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Newspaper sales combine nominal independence with substantial control
sections.cue: What was the workers’ actual relationship with publishers?
paragraphs: Four Los Angeles daily newspapers distributed through regular street vendors, conventionally called newsboys but generally mature men working steadily over long periods, relying on sales for livelihood and often supporting families. Their position differed from children and casual sellers. The dispute concerned these street vendors, not every newsstand, independent dealer, or home-delivery carrier.

District managers coordinated sales and delivery by area. Checkmen or main-spot vendors sometimes redistributed papers and collected receipts for small salaries while spending most of their time selling. Other vendors earned the spread between purchase and retail prices, but publishers effectively controlled that spread and influenced earnings through territory and allocation. Papers usually came on credit with return privileges, although exceptions and losses on unreturned copies existed. Managers could impose quantities rather than leaving absolute choice.

Managers assigned spots, could transfer sellers, substantially prescribed hours, supervised work, and reprimanded or dismissed them. Publishers supplied equipment, advertisements, and display and sales instructions. Countervailing features included sales of competing publications, transfers of locations, relief workers, some financial losses, and absence of normal payroll or insurance classifications. Classification required evaluating both sides of the arrangement.

sources.pinpoint: Workers and distribution; 322 U.S. at 113–20 & nn.10–17

sections.title: Union elections and refused bargaining generate four enforcement cases
sections.cue: What did the Board decide and the circuit reject?
paragraphs: The Los Angeles Newsboys union petitioned the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) for investigation and certification. After a consolidated hearing, the Board classified regular full-time vendors as employees, selected units, and ordered elections. The union won majorities and was certified. The four papers refused to bargain, asserting independent-contractor status.

Subsequent unfair-labor-practice proceedings produced cease-and-desist and bargaining orders. Consolidating representation proceedings did not mean evidence about one paper was indiscriminately applied to another. The record supported separate employer findings.

The Ninth Circuit, with one judge dissenting, independently applied what it considered common-law employment standards and set aside the orders. In Supreme Court review, publishers also challenged unit selection and evidence sufficiency, but abandoned their earlier no-effect-on-commerce contention.

sources.pinpoint: Administrative and judicial procedure; 322 U.S. at 114–20 & nn.3–6, 18

sections.title: Rutledge rejects exclusive control by labels developed for other legal purposes
sections.cue: Why did national coverage require more than a supposed uniform common law?
paragraphs: Justice Rutledge found no single simple common-law test doing the work publishers claimed. Classifications varied among jurisdictions and contexts such as tort liability and social legislation. Using local rules would give otherwise similar workers different coverage under the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA), a national response to national labor problems. Extracting a general essence would still import technical categories designed for other ends.

The Court did not include every service provider or make legal classifications irrelevant. It identified an intermediate zone between clear employment and clear entrepreneurship. There the Act’s concerns—labor unrest, unequal bargaining power, and practical collective organization—supplied perspective. Workers labeled contractors elsewhere might have the same dependence and inability to bargain individually that motivated statutory protection.

Broad definitions and history supported reaching beyond a narrow master-servant model. Examples of collective organization among other atypical occupations reinforced the inadequacy of labels, not a holding that every member of each occupation was an employee.

sections.title: The Court distinguishes interpretation from the Board’s initial factual application
sections.cue: What made this classification reviewable but sustainable?
paragraphs: Statutory interpretation remained judicial work with appropriate respect for administrative judgment. Applying a broad term initially to a specific economic relationship, however, fell within the Board’s experienced administration of industries, workers, and bargaining disputes. Reviewing courts should not substitute their own inferences for supported agency findings.

The classification needed a warrant in the record and a reasonable legal basis. Regular work, dependence, publisher influence over markets and prices, supervision, and furnished equipment supplied both. The Court did not defer merely because the agency said “employee”; it assessed the factual findings against its own understanding of the statutory purposes before sustaining the application.

sources.pinpoint: Court and agency roles; 322 U.S. at 130–32

sections.title: The Board can draw practical units around stable organized workers
sections.cue: Why did exclusions not make these units arbitrary?
paragraphs: Units generally included regular full-time street sellers and sometimes checkmen, excluding bootjackers and temporary, casual, or part-time vendors. The papers used different practical criteria, such as regular sales of particular editions or established spots for four hours daily and five days weekly. Stable tenure could matter more than identical tasks, and mathematical precision was unnecessary where peripheral hypothetical exceptions did not undermine workable units.

Some suburban sellers were excluded because organization had not reached them. There was no evidence of deliberately rejected applicants or suburban interest, and no competing union sought them. Congress gave the Board flexibility to make bargaining practical. The Court saw no reason to withhold protection from an organized group until geographically separated sellers chose participation. It approved this supported exercise rather than arbitrary exclusions generally.

sections.title: Reed states a narrower agreement and Roberts defends the ordinary legal category
sections.cue: How did the separate positions differ?
paragraphs: Justice Reed concurred in the result, identifying the Board’s Stockholders Publishing coverage test as proper without joining every majority formulation.

Justice Roberts would affirm the Ninth Circuit. He considered “employee” an established term whose interpretation belonged to judges. The alternative need not mechanically reproduce each state’s local law, he argued. Congress had not authorized the Board to redefine employment to achieve its own policy preferences. Statutory references to employees of different employers protected cross-employer union organization, not agency conversion of nonemployees into employees.

sections.title: The Board’s employee and unit determinations survive Supreme Court review
sections.cue: What does the historical judgment establish?
paragraphs: On April 24, 1944, the Supreme Court reversed and remanded all four causes for proceedings consistent with its opinion, eight to one. The designated employee classifications had evidentiary and legal support, and the unit distinctions fell within Board discretion.

Later assigned deference discussions, including opposing accounts in Loper Bright, highlight different portions of Hearst. Those later descriptions do not replace its combination of judicial statutory interpretation and limited review of particular agency application. This judgment applies the 1944 statutory setting and does not establish classification under later legislation or amendments.

sources.pinpoint: Judgment and assigned scope; 322 U.S. at 132–37
